```{r, include = FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(
  collapse = TRUE,
  comment = "#>",
  fig.width = 7,
  fig.height = 5,
  dpi = 96,
  dev = "jpeg",
  dev.args = list(quality = 90),
  out.width = "100%"
)
has_shazam <- requireNamespace("shazam", quietly = TRUE)
# SIRUP_IMGT_DIR is the human "vdj" folder. imgt_refs is the folder that downloadIMGT() makes.
imgt_vdj <- path.expand(Sys.getenv("SIRUP_IMGT_DIR"))
imgt_refs <- dirname(dirname(imgt_vdj))
has_imgt <- nzchar(imgt_vdj) && dir.exists(file.path(imgt_refs, "human", "vdj")) && has_shazam
has_trees <- has_imgt
```

<div markdown="1" style="background: #F7E5BC; padding: 12px; margin-bottom: 24px; line-height: 24px;">
  <p style="margin: -12px -12px 12px; padding: 6px 12px; background: #d6b676; color: #ffffff; font-weight: 700;"> <b>Note</b> </p>
  **Time:** ~15 minutes.<br>
  **Data:** The example SIRUP object, plus its polygon file.<br>
</div>

Here, we will work with the clones in a SIRUP object, build lineage trees for some of them, and pair each tree with the tissue.

A *clone* is a group of B or T cells that descend from one ancestor cell and share its receptor rearrangement. A *lineage tree* shows how the sequences of one clone relate to each other, where each tip is one sequence.
Pairing a tree with the tissue shows where each tip sits. At the end, we will compare distances in the tree with distances on the tissue.

SIRUP does not reimplement clone calling or tree building. It runs the Immcantation tools (scoper, dowser, shazam) on the receptor table inside the SIRUP object, then adds the spatial part: clone maps, trees paired with
tissue plots, and distances between tips in and between regions.

<div markdown="1" style="background: #F7E5BC; padding: 12px; margin-bottom: 24px; line-height: 24px;">
  <p style="margin: -12px -12px 12px; padding: 6px 12px; background: #d6b676; color: #ffffff; font-weight: 700;"> <b>Note</b> </p>
  This page starts with a saved SIRUP object, which is loaded below. To learn how the object is built, see `vignette("get-started", package = "SIRUP")`. To learn about the polygons used here, see `vignette("regions", package = "SIRUP")`.
</div>

## Get the example data

This page uses example files that are slightly too big to be part of the SIRUP package. This code
downloads them. Change `dest` to a folder you want to keep. The function skips files that are already there.

```{r download-data, message = FALSE}
extdata <- SIRUP::downloadSIRUPExample(
  dest = file.path(tempdir(), "SIRUP_example"),
  files = c(
    "mg_thymus_slice2_brighter.sirup.rds",
    "mg_thymus_slice2_gc_polygons.csv"
  )
)
```

```{r libraries, message = FALSE, warning = FALSE}
library(SIRUP)
library(dplyr)
library(ggplot2)
```

```{r setup}
sirup <- readSIRUP(file.path(extdata, "mg_thymus_slice2_brighter.sirup.rds"))
sirup
```

The object holds two receptor slots, `"BCR"` and `"TCR"`, and the functions that interact with the receptors in the SIRUP
object read one slot at a time. If we only need to work with one type of receptor, we can specify the slot in the function call.

In `vignette("regions", package = "SIRUP")`, we annotated regions of interest (ROIs) in the tissue. We can add the polygons
that outline these ROIs to the SIRUP object so that we can include them in plots and analyses. Add the polygons to the
object with `addPolygons()`.

```{r add-polygons}
sirup <- addPolygons(
  sirup,
  polygons_path = file.path(extdata, "mg_thymus_slice2_gc_polygons.csv")
)
```

## Build clones

A clone, or clonal lineage, is a set of cells inferred to have descended from a common ancestor. We can infer clones from
the receptor sequences using `scoper::hierarchicalClones()` for B cells and `scoper::identicalClones()` for T cells. 
Use the `updateReceptors()` function to run a function on the receptor table in a SIRUP object and update the object with the result. 

The example object already has BCR clones from `vignette("get-started", package = "SIRUP")`. To start from scratch,
we will remove the `clone_id` column and clear the clone field first.

```{r remove-clones}
sirup <- updateReceptors(
  sirup,
  dplyr::select,
  -clone_id,
  slot = "BCR", # specify the receptor slot
  receptor_fields = list(clone = NULL)
)
```

Then build the clones.

```{r clones, message = FALSE}
sirup <- updateReceptors(
  sirup,
  scoper::hierarchicalClones,
  slot = "BCR",
  threshold = 0.1,
  summarize_clones = FALSE,
  nproc = 1
)

sirup
```

Because T cells do not mutate their TCRs, clones are called with `scoper::identicalClones()`, as is below. 

```{r tcr-clones, message = FALSE}
sirup <- updateReceptors(
  sirup,
  scoper::identicalClones,
  slot = "TCR",
  summarize_clones = FALSE,
  nproc = 1
)
```

## Reconstruct clonal germlines

Next, reconstruct the germline of the B cell clones with `dowser::createGermlines()`. The germline is the sequence of the unmutated
common ancestor, which will root the reconstructed trees. Building the germline
requires IMGT references. Use the `imgt_refs` folder that you made with `downloadIMGT()` in the
[IgBLAST and IMGT germline references](processing.md#igblast-and-imgt-germline-references)
section of the processing guide.

<div markdown="1" style="background: #F7E5BC; padding: 12px; margin-bottom: 24px; line-height: 24px;">
  <p style="margin: -12px -12px 12px; padding: 6px 12px; background: #d6b676; color: #ffffff; font-weight: 700;"> <b>Note</b> </p>
  If you have not yet set up the IMGT references, follow the instructions in the
  [IgBLAST and IMGT germline references](processing.md#igblast-and-imgt-germline-references)
  section of the processing guide, which will create the `imgt_refs` folder.
  For more detail, see the
  [airrblast documentation](https://github.com/hoehnlab/airrblast).
</div>

```{r germlines, eval = has_imgt, message = FALSE}
# imgt_refs is the folder name from downloadIMGT()
references <- dowser::readIMGT(file.path(imgt_refs, "human", "vdj"))

sirup <- updateReceptors(
  sirup,
  dowser::createGermlines,
  slot = "BCR",
  references = references,
  id = "sequence_id",
  nproc = 1
)
```

To be safe, we can also filter out potential PCR chimeras using `shazam::slideWindowDb()`. 

```{r pcr chimeras, eval = has_shazam, message = FALSE}
sirup <- updateReceptors(sirup, slot = "BCR", function(receptors) {
  chimera <- shazam::slideWindowDb(
    receptors,
    sequenceColumn = "sequence_alignment",
    germlineColumn = "germline_alignment_d_mask",
    mutThresh = 6,
    windowSize = 10
  )
  receptors[!chimera, ]
})
```

## Estimate somatic hypermutation levels

Use `shazam::observedMutations()` to count the SHM levels of each sequence against the germline. 

```{r shm, eval = has_shazam}
sirup <- updateReceptors(
  sirup,
  shazam::observedMutations,
  slot = "BCR",
  sequenceColumn = "sequence_alignment",
  germlineColumn = "germline_alignment_d_mask",
  frequency = TRUE,
  combine = TRUE
)
summary(getReceptors(sirup, slot = "BCR")$mu_freq) # SHM frequency stored in mu_freq column
```

`plotReceptors()` can color spots by a numeric column in the receptor data. Pass the column to `value`. If a spot has
several receptors, `value_combine` sets how SIRUP combines them (default is `"mean"`).

```{r shm-map, eval = has_shazam}
plotReceptors(
  sirup,
  slot = "BCR",
  group = "locus",
  value = "mu_freq",
  value_colors = c("white", "darkred"),
  value_combine = "mean",
  receptor_size = 1.3,
  polygons = TRUE,
  polygon_alpha = 0,
  polygon_color = "black",
  title = "Mean SHM frequency per spot"
)
```

## Estimate trees

First, we need to choose a few clones to build trees for. The three clones below are large and have sequences in the 
ectopic germinal centers (the ROIs).

```{r choose-clones}
tree_clones <- c("739", "810", "196")

# Plot the locations of the three chosen clones
plotReceptors(
  sirup,
  slot = "BCR",
  group = "clone_id",
  group_val = tree_clones,
  receptor_size = 1.6,
  polygons = TRUE,
  polygon_alpha = 0.3,
  title = "Selected clones"
)
```

To build trees with Dowser, we need a formatted clones object. `formatSpatialClones()` wraps `dowser::formatClones()` 
but allows users to provide a SIRUP object, and it automatically places a `formatted_clones` object in the SIRUP object's
analysis slot. Then, we can call `getSpatialTrees()`, which wraps `dowser::getTrees()` but allows users to provide a SIRUP
object, and puts the trees in the SIRUP object's analysis slot. 

```{r build-trees, eval = has_trees}
# Filter the SIRUP object to only include the tree clones
tree_sirup <- updateReceptors(sirup, dplyr::filter, clone_id %in% tree_clones, slot = "BCR")

tree_sirup <- formatSpatialClones(
  tree_sirup,
  slot = "BCR",
  analysis_name = "formatted_clones",
  id = "sequence_id",
  germ = "germline_alignment_d_mask",
  traits = c("barcode_10x", "polygon_id") # Make sure to set the barcode column as a trait so that you don't collapse
  # sequences with the same sequence that were observed in different locations.
)

set.seed(1)
tree_sirup <- getSpatialTrees(
  tree_sirup,
  slot = "BCR",
  f_clones_analysis = "formatted_clones",
  analysis_name = "trees",
  build = "pratchet"
)

trees <- getAnalysis(tree_sirup, "trees")
trees
```

For more information on building trees, see the [Dowser documentation](https://dowser.readthedocs.io/en/stable/vignettes/Building-Trees-Vignette/).

```{r store-trees, eval = has_trees}
sirup <- setAnalysis(sirup, "trees", trees)
```

## Pair each tree with the tissue

`plotSpatialCloneTreePairs()` plots trees on the left and H\&E images and the locations of the tip sequences on the right. 
`color_by` allows you to color the tips on the tree by a column in the receptor data, but leaving it `NULL` gives each tip
its own color.

```{r tree-pairs, eval = has_trees, fig.width = 9, fig.height = 5}
pairs <- plotSpatialCloneTreePairs(
  getAnalysis(tree_sirup, "trees"),
  object = sirup,
  slot = "BCR",
  clone_val = tree_clones,
  id = "sequence_id",
  polygons = TRUE,
  polygon_alpha = 0,
  polygon_color = "black"
)
names(pairs)

pairs[[1]]
```

The result is a list with one element for each clone, and each element consists of the tree on the left and the map on the right.
Each element also holds the `tree` plot and the `spatial_clone` plot, which can be accessed separately for a custom layout.
Sequences in the same spot share a point on the map.

### Color tips by group

A clone with many tips can be hard to read when each tip has its own color. `clusterTreesTips()` cuts each tree into 
`k` connected groups of related tips. The code below uses `k = 4` for every tree. Then `plotSpatialCloneTreePairs()` 
with `color_by = "tree_cluster"` colors the tips by their corresponding cluster for easier visualization.

```{r tree-clusters, eval = has_trees, fig.width = 12, fig.height = 5.5}
clustered <- clusterTreesTips(
  trees,
  k = 4,
  id = "sequence_id",
  cluster = "tree_cluster" # What column to store the cluster assignments in
)

cluster_pairs <- plotSpatialCloneTreePairs(
  clustered,
  object = sirup,
  slot = "BCR",
  clone_val = tree_clones,
  id = "sequence_id",
  color_by = "tree_cluster",
  polygons = TRUE,
  polygon_alpha = 0,
  polygon_color = "black",
  show_spatial_legend = FALSE
)

cluster_pairs[[1]]
```


`color_by` accepts any column of the dowser clone data. For example, `color_by = "polygon_id"` colors each tip by which
polygon it belongs to.

<div markdown="1" style="background: #F7E5BC; padding: 12px; margin-bottom: 24px; line-height: 24px;">
  <p style="margin: -12px -12px 12px; padding: 6px 12px; background: #d6b676; color: #ffffff; font-weight: 700;"> <b>Tip</b> </p>
